children: By Hannah Erin Lang and Sam Goldfarb
The wheels are coming off the AI trade.

And for the first time since ChatGPT's late 2022 release ushered in a new era for the world-changing technology and the markets, nothing could persuade investors this week that the selloff was merely a speed bump on the road to AI's glittering future.

Not even the biggest IPO in history, from the purest play of the AI industry, Anthropic, could stop the bleeding. By Friday afternoon, most of the initial pop from the offering had washed away — along with the Nasdaq composite's entire gains for the year. This week alone, the tech-heavy benchmark's members lost more than $4 trillion in market value.

A fierce public backlash is threatening the construction of data centers. Nvidia's star CEO is out of a job. Anthropic's IPO fizzled. In a different moment, investors might have powered through each of those setbacks, focusing instead on AI's awesome growth potential. But the cracks in Wall Street's all-consuming tech bet have been deepening for months — and this week, they grew too big to ignore.
"There hasn't been one moment, but there also just hasn't been enough good news to offset" the bad news, said Alex Witten, co-head of Americas equities at Nomura.

Friday's feverish selling hit almost all of the major AI players, dragging every member of the Magnificent Seven lower and driving double-digit losses in neoclouds and chip makers. The Nasdaq fell 5.3%. Anthropic tumbled 8.5%. Nvidia shares, already in a tailspin, dropped 14% on the day.

For the week, the S&P 500 dropped 8.6%, closing in correction territory. The Nasdaq plunged 10%, capping its worst week since March 2020, when Covid first swept through the global economy, and the Dow industrials lost 8%. And the Cboe Volatility Index, the markets' "fear gauge," jumped to its highest level this year.
Wall Street was already rattled heading into the week, after a brutal stretch of selling. The next leg of the AI trade hung on developments for two of the biggest players.

Nvidia's earnings report Tuesday beat estimates, but investors seemed less concerned with numbers than getting more clarity on the fallout on the scandal that felled CEO Jensen Huang. They didn't get it, and Nvidia's selloff continued, dragging down a parade of stocks tied to its fortunes.
Then attention turned to Anthropic. For about two minutes on Thursday, it looked as though the stock-market's all-consuming bet on artificial intelligence was back in business.

When shares of the AI startup hit the tape in its $1.3 trillion initial public offering, shares immediately jumped 34% above the listing price. Green candles flickered across traders' computers screens. Individual investors watched, some with their cursor already hovering on the "buy" button.

Then, almost as quickly, the early gains reversed. Anthropic still closed higher in its first day, but limped into the close well below its session high. The selling accelerated Friday, leaving Anthropic shares just barely above their initial listing price.

Some traders described it as a bumpy but necessary shift, as the market transitions from one no-brainer phase of the AI investing boom to another. Others worried that investors are turning their backs on — or at least re-evaluating — the companies and industries that have underpinned market gains for the better part of four years.

"There's cracks, and then things break down. What we're seeing is when things break down," said John Davi, chief investment officer at Astoria Investment Management. Many of the investors he's spoken with are loaded up on tech and growth stocks, he said.
"I think those days are over."
'On all the time'
A few days before the midterm election, Don Calcagni had a feeling the results would rattle markets. He told his team at Mercer Advisors to clear their calendars.

His prediction proved correct — and the firm has been "firing on all cylinders" ever since, Calcagni said. The chief investment officer has been working regular 15-hour days and waking up in the middle of the night to check the headlines.
"You're really on all the time, and you're taking short rests to eat and sleep," he said. "This is really an all-hands-on-deck moment."

Even before the midterm election sent stocks on a roller-coaster ride, Wall Street's AI jitters had grown. Investors fretted about growing debt burdens at neocloud companies that rent out computing capacity and the shrinking cash reserves at tech giants such as Alphabet.
Then the midterms crystallized a wave of AI backlash and scandal hit at Nvidia. From there, the list of worries only grew: A series of tech outages stoked fears about AI-powered cyberattacks.
That series of events left investors questioning the profit estimates for the companies at the center of the AI build-out, said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services.

"The big picture is that we are seeing something of a buyers' strike," Lerner said. "I would not say investors have lost confidence in AI's long-term potential. But they have lost confidence in the earnings forecasts supporting the AI trade."
Looking to the Fed

Jim Russo, portfolio manager at AllianceBernstein, said his team started shedding holdings of semiconductor stocks and other beneficiaries of AI infrastructure spending in the summer. They have turned more negative on the sector since then based on a belief that the growth rate of AI spending has already started to slow and will continue to decelerate in the coming years.

Spending, Russo said, is being constrained by three main factors: uncertainty about the profitability of frontier AI labs; rising funding costs for companies; and a public backlash making it harder to build data centers.
"All three of the constraints have gotten worse, and that has directly led to a derisking" across the tech sector, he said.
As stocks have sold off in recent days, investors have increasingly wondered if they could get help from the Federal Reserve.

The Fed has been anything but helpful to markets. It lifted interest rates in September for the first time in three years, and expectations for further hikes have pushed up U.S. Treasury yields. That has hurt stocks by both lifting corporate borrowing costs and tempting investors to buy bonds instead of riskier assets.

Some see parallels to 2018, when the Fed was raising rates, Democrats did well in November midterms, and stocks fell sharply at the end of the year. In that case, the Fed raised rates once more in December but then quickly pivoted to a dovish posture, prompting an immediate rebound in stocks.
A key difference now is that inflation has been stuck for years above the Fed's 2% target, making the central bank less sensitive to the market's concerns.

Giving investors some hope, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has talked often about the importance of financial conditions to the economy. That could make him less inclined to support rate increases if stock prices are falling.
Other officials, though, have sounded more hawkish recently, expressing growing concern that inflation is moving in the wrong direction.

There are officials saying, "we're five years over our target, we've got to get inflation down, and I think they will be much less deterred by this financial conditions argument," said John Briggs, head of U.S. rates strategy at Natixis Corporate & Investment Banking.
